newsitem.title: FRANCE: France firm on deficit as press zooms on pressures.
newsitem.headline: France firm on deficit as press zooms on pressures.

text.p: Amid resurgent press speculation about French budget pressures, a finance ministry official said on Wednesday the government would cut its 1997 deficit by enough to join European monetary union (EMU) and saw no signs of slippage.

French newspapers are assessing state finances with renewed vigour in the run-up to a parliament debate in May on the 1998 budget, with the authoritative Le Monde newspaper suggesting on Wednesday that more belt-tightening would be needed this year.

"The government will achieve its objectives, that is, three percent," the finance ministry official said, referring to the criterion of reducing 1997 public deficits to three percent of gross domestic product to join a single euro currency in 1999.
As Finance Minister Jean Arthuis had said recently, the government "will do what is necessary" in any case to make sure that goal is met, the official said.

Le Monde said the finance ministry's budget and forecasting divisions had carried out simulations which hinted at risks of a bigger social security deficit than expected and weaker revenues and, as a result, a risk of the 1997 public deficit overshooting the three percent target fairly markedly.

Given the centre-right government's determination to ensure it passes the critical test for joining a single currency, the government could well have to consider turning the screws further on 1997 finances than so far planned.

"According to our information, the budget and forecasting services of the finance ministry -- the former in a more alarmist tone -- have presented simulations to the government which hint that France could quite markedly overshoot the three percent deficit target with unchanged policy," Le Monde said.

Among the risks cited were weak revenues, notably weak value-added tax receipts in the last months of 1996 and early months of 1997, signs of growth based more on foreign than domestic demand as well as the social security deficit.

"Reliable sources" said the government's deficit reduction programme had been based on expectations the wage bill would progress by around four percent this year, but the trend at the moment looked headed for a rise limited to around three percent.
The government was counting on a social security deficit of 30 billion francs but the wage trend risked increasing this.
"If this (wage) trend proved more lasting, the lost revenues for the social security could be around 10 or 12 billion."

Prime Minister Alain Juppe met heads of French political parties and the parliament's influential finance committee for lunch on Tuesday in preparation for the 1998 budget debate in the National Assembly on May 13-14.

Arthuis has already said he will freeze about 10 billion francs of 1997 spending credits as a precaution against any overshoot in a budget which has already capped 1997 spending at the previous year's levels.
"But in government circles, people are not hiding the fact it may be necessary to consider turning the screws further, if there is slippage in the next two months," Le Monde said.
Further belt-tightening could hit plans by Labour Minister Jacques Barrot to extend to other low wage sectors a textile industry scheme which allows employers to contribute less in payroll charges.
The finance ministry official pointed to the announcement on Tuesday that the budget deficit at the end of February was 72.4 billion francs, versus 90 billion at the same stage last year.
Nothing so far cast any doubt on the government's aims, said the official said.

The government is already bracing for another tough budget for 1998 given the European Union "stability pact" designed to make sure state finances are kept strictly in trim well after countries make it through the 1997 fitness test.
